# Colon diverticular disease and lower-GI bleeding

## Assignment

- Topic `colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding`, wave 3. Colon — diverticular disease and lower GI bleeding.
- Included scope. Diverticulitis, diverticular complications, elective sigmoid decisions, diverticular bleeding and other nonmalignant lower-GI hemorrhage.
- Boundaries. Cancer, polyps and colonoscopy lesion work belong to colorectal-polyps-cancer. IBD belongs to bowel-ibd-malabsorption-short-bowel. Anorectal bleeding belongs to anorectal-benign-pelvic-floor.
- Priority high. Common colonic emergencies and post-recovery decisions support practical multi-stage cases.
- Starting topic supply comprises 4 live concepts, 16 live nodes in 8 cases, and 2 retained draft rows. Existing unkeyed slots and registry-only default identities both total 0.
- Initial repository baseline comprises 145 manifest rows, 1,151 cases, 1,462 nodes and 610 registered concepts. Program capture `2026-11-11T15:28:05.732Z` under `question-ship.2026-11-10.v9`.
- Current shared release recheck found `question-ship.2026-11-11.v10`, 167 manifest rows, 1167 cases, 1482 nodes and 631 registered concepts. All 16 assigned live nodes remain present. All four assigned source-definition modules retain their captured hashes.
- Frozen independent PASS references and exact clinical approvals in this assignment both total 0. The existing retained drop proposal `review.n3.postdiverticulitis-examination-extent.v2` remains recorded.
- Manager coordination follows `docs/handoffs/CURRENT_THREAD_HANDOFF.md; topic program wave 3`. Melissa Rowland is named clinical sign-off.

The owner requested more difficult, accurate questions, stronger existing questions and consequential gap coverage, with natural multi-decision cases where appropriate. Hospital decisions appear through named patient chart reviews in the existing clinic setting.

Full bibliographic, authority, reuse and limitation records remain in <code>docs/research/sources-question-topic-colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding-20261111.json</code>. The ledger adds only the three exact context mappings.

Each new case has one fixed named patient profile, one existing stable concept and one scored node in the existing clinic. All nine testing choices, including distractors, keep their exact choice identity/label and prior placeholder timing profile. Proposed orders remain not_executed / future_planned, with null services and result gates. No shared registry, manifest, runtime, selector or save is edited.

The two first-episode investigations reuse the same CT concept meaning; alarm colonoscopy reuses its existing meaning. These are isolated case contexts, not new concepts or question variants. Standalone selection removes the non-PASS companion dependency without altering FSRS eligibility. The original held urinary context remains exact for audit; the new standalone context resolves its proposed terminal-metadata assembly issue pending review.

  Rationale: The catheter reaches a collapsed cavity. Increasing its size does not establish access to the separate enlarging collection.
  Distractor rationale: The catheter reaches a collapsed cavity. Increasing its size does not establish access to the separate enlarging collection.

Explanation: The new collection lies outside the drained space. The combination of clinical worsening and an inaccessible enlarging source supports operative source control. A larger catheter in the collapsed cavity does not repair the anatomic mismatch.

- Current update: After resuscitation, exploration found a disrupted sigmoid diverticulum with a visible full-thickness opening and liquid stool in several abdominal compartments. The remaining colon was viable. Broad-spectrum antibiotics had already been given.

Options ? key shown first for review only:

- **Attempted key** <code>choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.gross-perforation-source-control.resection.v1</code>: Resect the perforated diseased sigmoid segment
  Rationale: The gross perforation and fecal contamination favor removal of the diseased source.
- Distractor <code>choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.gross-perforation-source-control.lavage.v1</code>: Perform peritoneal lavage and place abdominal drains
  Rationale: A visible perforation with diffuse fecal contamination requires control of the diseased bowel source. Evidence for selected lavage in purulent disease does not support this feculent presentation.
  Distractor rationale: A visible perforation with diffuse fecal contamination requires control of the diseased bowel source. Evidence for selected lavage in purulent disease does not support this feculent presentation.
- Distractor <code>choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.gross-perforation-source-control.repair.v1</code>: Close the visible opening and place abdominal drains

- Finite profiles: [{"id":"profile.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.immunosuppressed-recovery.v2","prototypeDemographics":{"ageYears":68,"sexLabel":"Female"},"chiefComplaint":"Treatment follow-up","presentation":"{patientName}, a 68-year-old woman, attends clinic to review her first sigmoid inflammatory episode. Her records document a kidney transplant treated with tacrolimus and mycophenolate and chronic lung disease requiring home oxygen."}]
- Current update: The admitting team had already chosen ward observation. CT showed focal sigmoid thickening and fat inflammation without a collection or free perforation. She was alert with normal pulse and blood pressure, tolerated food and tablets without vomiting, and reported improving pain. Tacrolimus and mycophenolate were continued. She had no penicillin allergy and renal function was preserved. Each medication plan would use the same observation and reassessment arrangements.
- Complete task: **Which oral medication plan best fits {patientName}'s acute hospital assessment?**

Options ? key shown first for review only:

- **Attempted key** <code>choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.immunosuppressed-antibiotic-decision.oral-antibiotic.v2</code>: Use oral amoxicillin-clavulanate
  Rationale: Immune suppression supports antibiotics despite limited CT disease. Amoxicillin-clavulanate is a listed complete oral regimen while the selected observation continues.
- Distractor <code>choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.immunosuppressed-antibiotic-decision.support.v2</code>: Use oral hydration and analgesia
  Rationale: Limited CT disease does not make a transplant recipient on immune suppression eligible for routine antibiotic omission.
  Distractor rationale: Limited CT disease does not make a transplant recipient on immune suppression eligible for routine antibiotic omission.
- Distractor <code>choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.immunosuppressed-antibiotic-decision.ciprofloxacin.v2</code>: Use oral ciprofloxacin
  Rationale: The listed ciprofloxacin-based diverticulitis regimen pairs it with metronidazole. The offered entire plan omits that anaerobic component.
  Distractor rationale: The listed ciprofloxacin-based diverticulitis regimen pairs it with metronidazole. The offered entire plan omits that anaerobic component.

Explanation: Uncomplicated imaging does not erase the antibiotic indication from immune suppression. With observation held common and oral tolerance established, amoxicillin-clavulanate is the supported offered oral regimen. A ciprofloxacin-based diverticulitis plan includes an anaerobic partner. Admission, intravenous route, dose and duration are not decided here.

- Patient Helen Shaw; demographics {"ageYears":68,"sexLabel":"Female"}.
- Complaint: Treatment follow-up
- Presentation: {patientName}, a 68-year-old woman, attends clinic to review her first sigmoid inflammatory episode. Her records document a kidney transplant treated with tacrolimus and mycophenolate and chronic lung disease requiring home oxygen.
- Finite profiles: [{"id":"profile.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.immunosuppressed-recovery.v2","prototypeDemographics":{"ageYears":68,"sexLabel":"Female"},"chiefComplaint":"Treatment follow-up","presentation":"{patientName}, a 68-year-old woman, attends clinic to review her first sigmoid inflammatory episode. Her records document a kidney transplant treated with tacrolimus and mycophenolate and chronic lung disease requiring home oxygen."}]
- Current update: She returned to her usual bowel pattern after the first episode and had no further attacks. CT showed no collection or narrowing. She used home oxygen, stopped to rest while crossing a room and needed help bathing. She wanted to preserve independence and avoid both an emergency operation and prolonged postoperative loss of function; she had not ranked those competing risks.
- Complete task: **Which elective plan best fits {patientName}'s recovered clinic assessment?**
- Preceding visible explanations: Uncomplicated imaging does not erase the antibiotic indication from immune suppression. With observation held common and oral tolerance established, amoxicillin-clavulanate is the supported offered oral regimen. A ciprofloxacin-based diverticulitis plan includes an anaerobic partner. Admission, intravenous route, dose and duration are not decided here.

Options ? key shown first for review only (attempted key is audit-only; excluded from preview):

- **Attempted key** <code>choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.high-risk-recovered-observation.observe.v2</code>: Arrange nonoperative follow-up
  Rationale: Absent recurrent burden and major functional limitations make observation reasonable, but the guideline does not uniquely mandate it without the individualized decision.
- Distractor <code>choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.high-risk-recovered-observation.colectomy.v2</code>: Arrange elective sigmoid resection
  Rationale: Transplant status prompts individualized discussion, not automatic surgery. Functional and operative tradeoffs remain unresolved.
  Distractor rationale: Transplant status prompts individualized discussion, not automatic surgery. Functional and operative tradeoffs remain unresolved.
- Distractor <code>choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.high-risk-recovered-observation.optimize.v2</code>: Arrange pulmonary optimization before surgical reassessment
  Rationale: Further assessment can reasonably precede an operative decision, competing with observation in this incomplete tradeoff.
  Distractor rationale: Further assessment can reasonably precede an operative decision, competing with observation in this incomplete tradeoff.

Explanation: Recovery, absent recurrence and major functional limitations all matter. Immune suppression alone does not settle elective surgery. This attempt is parked because the competing priorities remain unranked and several next strategies are reasonable.

  Rationale: Ongoing significant blood loss offers a chance to localize active bleeding without requiring bowel preparation.
- Distractor <code>choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.ongoing-bleeding-cta.colonoscopy.v1</code>: Colonoscopy after another attempt at full bowel preparation

  Distractor rationale: Scintigraphy can help with intermittent bleeding. CTA offers a more useful prompt anatomic localization route for this continuing significant hemorrhage.

Explanation: The repeated blood loss and circulatory response establish an ongoing significant bleed. After assessment of the upper tract, CTA is the proposed localization study while resuscitation continues. The bleeding phase and preparation failure determine the choice.

- Current update: On CTA, the ascending-colon lumen contained no dense focus before contrast. A new focus appeared during the arterial phase and enlarged into the lumen on the later phase. He continued to pass blood and require resuscitation. The earlier preparation had not cleared the colon.
- Complete task: **Which next hemostatic plan best fits {patientName}'s CTA and continuing course?**
- Preceding visible explanations: The repeated blood loss and circulatory response establish an ongoing significant bleed. After assessment of the upper tract, CTA is the proposed localization study while resuscitation continues. The bleeding phase and preparation failure determine the choice.

- **Attempted key** <code>choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.nonbleeding-vessel-treatment.clip.v2</code>: Apply endoscopic clips and end local treatment
  Rationale: A reachable residual vessel is a high-risk target despite stopped flow. Clips are an accepted second modality after temporary injection control.
- Distractor <code>choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.nonbleeding-vessel-treatment.observe.v2</code>: Wash the site and end local treatment
  Rationale: Stopped flow after injection does not remove the high-risk residual vessel. Ending treatment leaves durable hemostasis unresolved.

  Distractor rationale: Further injection still makes epinephrine the endpoint. It can aid visualization but should not be the final modality for the persistent vessel.

Explanation: Injection changed flow and visibility, but an exposed vessel remained. Complete hemostasis with an accepted second modality such as clips instead of stopping with observation or epinephrine alone.

- Finite profiles: [{"id":"profile.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.recurrent-localized-hemorrhage.v1","prototypeDemographics":{"ageYears":70,"sexLabel":"Male"},"chiefComplaint":"Recurrent bleeding review","presentation":"{patientName}, a 70-year-old man, attends clinic after an outside admission for recurrent colonic bleeding. The founder reviews the endoscopic, radiologic and surgical records in sequence."}]
- Current update: A prepared colonoscopy had treated an actively bleeding ascending-colon diverticulum with clips. Later, recurrent large bloody stools required further transfusion and fluid replacement. Repeat CTA showed active contrast accumulation beside the marked ascending-colon site. The colon had again filled with blood and clot, and his blood pressure fell during further bleeding.
- Complete task: **Which next hemostatic plan best fits {patientName}'s recurrent hospital bleeding?**

Options ? key shown first for review only:

- **Attempted key** <code>choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.rebleed-after-clipping.ir.v1</code>: Proceed to selective angiography with possible embolization
  Rationale: CTA localizes recurrent active bleeding after endoscopic treatment, and the continuing course is poorly suited to another preparation-dependent examination.
- Distractor <code>choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.rebleed-after-clipping.colonoscopy.v1</code>: Repeat full preparation and endoscopic hemostasis
  Rationale: Repeat colonoscopy is reasonable in selected stable prepared recurrences. The continuing significant blood loss and newly localized active source support radiologic hemostasis here.
  Distractor rationale: Repeat colonoscopy is reasonable in selected stable prepared recurrences. The continuing significant blood loss and newly localized active source support radiologic hemostasis here.
- Distractor <code>choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.rebleed-after-clipping.colectomy.v1</code>: Proceed directly to right colectomy for hemorrhage control
  Rationale: The localization makes surgery possible if needed. A radiologic treatment route remains to be attempted before surgical rescue.
  Distractor rationale: The localization makes surgery possible if needed. A radiologic treatment route remains to be attempted before surgical rescue.

Explanation: The recurrence is ongoing and hemodynamically significant after attempted endoscopic treatment. CTA supplies a current anatomic target. Selective angiography with possible embolization is the proposed next route.

- Finite profiles: [{"id":"profile.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.elective-resection-planning.v1","prototypeDemographics":{"ageYears":57,"sexLabel":"Female"},"chiefComplaint":"Surgery planning","presentation":"{patientName}, a 57-year-old woman, attends clinic to review the planned extent of elective surgery for recurrent sigmoid diverticulitis."}]
- Current update: Her disease was confined to a thickened, fibrotic sigmoid segment. The descending colon was soft and free of inflammation but contained scattered diverticula. The proximal rectum was healthy. The colon could reach the rectum without tension after mobilization. Preoperative colonic assessment found no other lesion requiring resection.
- Complete task: **Which resection plan best fits {patientName}'s operative anatomy?**

Options ? key shown first for review only:

- **Attempted key** <code>choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.healthy-resection-boundaries.sigmoid.v1</code>: Remove the diseased sigmoid and join descending colon to rectum
  Rationale: This removes the diseased sigmoid, uses a healthy proximal margin and reaches rectum. Uninflamed proximal diverticula do not by themselves justify additional resection.
- Distractor <code>choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.healthy-resection-boundaries.limited.v1</code>: Remove the thickened segment and join descending colon to distal sigmoid
  Rationale: Leaving distal sigmoid as the anastomotic target does not follow the recommended rectal distal boundary.
  Distractor rationale: Leaving distal sigmoid as the anastomotic target does not follow the recommended rectal distal boundary.
- Distractor <code>choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.healthy-resection-boundaries.extended.v1</code>: Remove sigmoid and descending colon and join transverse colon to rectum
  Rationale: Scattered diverticula in soft uninflamed descending colon do not establish a need to remove that additional segment.
  Distractor rationale: Scattered diverticula in soft uninflamed descending colon do not establish a need to remove that additional segment.

Explanation: Resection should remove the diseased sigmoid and use healthy proximal colon with a rectal distal target. Uninflamed proximal diverticula do not require an extended colectomy.

- Patient Mara Collins; demographics {"ageYears":57,"sexLabel":"Female"}.
- Complaint: Surgery planning
- Presentation: {patientName}, a 57-year-old woman, attends clinic after elective sigmoid surgery for recurrent diverticulitis. The clinic review examines the operative record.
- Finite profiles: [{"id":"profile.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.elective-resection-planning.v2","prototypeDemographics":{"ageYears":57,"sexLabel":"Female"},"chiefComplaint":"Surgery planning","presentation":"{patientName}, a 57-year-old woman, attends clinic after elective sigmoid surgery for recurrent diverticulitis. The clinic review examines the operative record."}]
- Current update: The completed operative report described a thickened fibrotic sigmoid segment. The descending colon was soft without inflammation but contained scattered diverticula. A short distal sigmoid segment felt soft. The proximal rectum was healthy, and mobilized descending colon reached it without tension. Preoperative assessment found no other lesion requiring removal. The clinic review compares the boundary plans considered during that operation.
- Complete task: **Which pair of transection targets best fits {patientName}'s operative findings?**

Options ? key shown first for review only:

- **Attempted key** <code>choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.healthy-resection-boundaries.sigmoid.v2</code>: Descending colon proximally; proximal rectum distally
  Rationale: Healthy descending colon need not be removed for uninflamed diverticula; healthy rectum supplies the supported distal target.
- Distractor <code>choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.healthy-resection-boundaries.limited.v2</code>: Descending colon proximally; distal sigmoid distally
  Rationale: The proximal target preserves uninvolved colon, but retained distal sigmoid is not the supported distal target for sigmoid diverticulitis resection.
  Distractor rationale: The proximal target preserves uninvolved colon, but retained distal sigmoid is not the supported distal target for sigmoid diverticulitis resection.
- Distractor <code>choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.healthy-resection-boundaries.extended.v2</code>: Transverse colon proximally; proximal rectum distally
  Rationale: The rectal target fits, but extension removes uninflamed descending colon for diverticula alone.
  Distractor rationale: The rectal target fits, but extension removes uninflamed descending colon for diverticula alone.
- Distractor <code>choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.healthy-resection-boundaries.extended-sigmoid.v2</code>: Transverse colon proximally; distal sigmoid distally
  Rationale: This combines unnecessary proximal extension with retention of distal sigmoid; both proposed targets need correction in this context.
  Distractor rationale: This combines unnecessary proximal extension with retention of distal sigmoid; both proposed targets need correction in this context.

Explanation: Assess each margin independently. Remove diseased sigmoid to a healthy rectal distal target while using healthy uninvolved proximal colon. Scattered diverticula in uninflamed descending colon do not require extension to transverse colon.

- Current update: The bleeding site was treated and there had been no further blood loss. Aspirin was prescribed after a documented myocardial infarction. He also used naproxen for knee pain. He was taking no other antiplatelet or anticoagulant drug.

Options ? key shown first for review only:

- **Attempted key** <code>choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.continue-secondary-aspirin.aspirin-stop-naproxen.v1</code>: Continue aspirin and discontinue naproxen

- Distractor <code>choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.continue-secondary-aspirin.both.v1</code>: Continue aspirin and continue naproxen
  Rationale: The cardiovascular aspirin indication remains, but nonaspirin NSAID exposure should be avoided when feasible after diverticular bleeding.
  Distractor rationale: The cardiovascular aspirin indication remains, but nonaspirin NSAID exposure should be avoided when feasible after diverticular bleeding.
- Distractor <code>choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.continue-secondary-aspirin.stop-aspirin.v1</code>: Discontinue aspirin and continue naproxen
  Rationale: This removes secondary cardiovascular prevention while retaining the avoidable NSAID exposure.
  Distractor rationale: This removes secondary cardiovascular prevention while retaining the avoidable NSAID exposure.
- Distractor <code>choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.continue-secondary-aspirin.stop-both.v1</code>: Discontinue aspirin and discontinue naproxen

  Distractor rationale: Avoiding naproxen fits the bleeding history, but the established cardiovascular aspirin indication still needs preservation after controlled bleeding.

Explanation: After secure hemostasis, aspirin for a documented prior myocardial infarction generally remains indicated. Nonaspirin NSAIDs should be avoided when feasible after diverticular hemorrhage. The medicine's indication determines which bleeding-risk tradeoff is justified.

Options ? key shown first for review only:

- **Attempted key** <code>choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.stop-primary-prevention-aspirin.stop.v1</code>: Discontinue daily aspirin after discharge
  Rationale: No established cardiovascular indication is recorded. Current lower-GI bleeding guidance supports discontinuing primary-prevention aspirin after this event.
- Distractor <code>choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.stop-primary-prevention-aspirin.continue.v1</code>: Continue daily aspirin after discharge
  Rationale: Her recorded use is primary prevention. After diverticular bleeding, that indication generally does not justify continued aspirin exposure.
  Distractor rationale: Her recorded use is primary prevention. After diverticular bleeding, that indication generally does not justify continued aspirin exposure.
- Distractor <code>choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.stop-primary-prevention-aspirin.substitute.v1</code>: Replace daily aspirin with daily clopidogrel
  Rationale: Substituting another antiplatelet agent does not establish an indication that was absent for aspirin.
  Distractor rationale: Substituting another antiplatelet agent does not establish an indication that was absent for aspirin.

Explanation: Risk factors and family history place aspirin in a primary-prevention role here. After diverticular hemorrhage, that role generally supports discontinuation. A different antiplatelet drug does not create a missing indication.

- Current update: During a well-prepared colonoscopy, several flat branching red vascular patches in the cecum slowly oozed blood after washing. The surrounding mucosa was intact. There was no focal exposed vessel within a diverticulum. Circulation remained stable during the examination.
- Complete task: **Which endoscopic treatment best fits {patientName}'s colonoscopy record?**

Options ? key shown first for review only:

- **Attempted key** <code>choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.flat-vascular-lesion-treatment.apc.v1</code>: Apply argon plasma coagulation to the bleeding patches
  Rationale: The report describes superficial vascular lesions consistent with angioectasia. Noncontact argon plasma coagulation is an accepted endoscopic treatment.
- Distractor <code>choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.flat-vascular-lesion-treatment.clip.v1</code>: Apply through-the-scope clips to the bleeding patches
  Rationale: Clips suit a discrete target such as a focal diverticular bleeding vessel. These broad superficial vascular patches call for a different endoscopic approach.
  Distractor rationale: Clips suit a discrete target such as a focal diverticular bleeding vessel. These broad superficial vascular patches call for a different endoscopic approach.
- Distractor <code>choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.flat-vascular-lesion-treatment.inject.v1</code>: Inject dilute epinephrine into the bleeding patches
  Rationale: Injection may give transient control but is not the definitive treatment proposed for these superficial vascular lesions.
  Distractor rationale: Injection may give transient control but is not the definitive treatment proposed for these superficial vascular lesions.

Explanation: The flat branching mucosal vascular pattern supports angioectasia. Argon plasma coagulation is an accepted noncontact treatment. A discrete diverticular vessel and a broad superficial vascular lesion call for different hemostatic approaches.

Current status: **revised**. Fair moderate rather than hard: interpret residual distributed oozing after focal control, then select an accepted feasible treatment for the remaining mucosal vascular target.

Changes: Remove tailored negative diverticular finding; Add a focal-treatment response; Avoid a universal modality hierarchy.

- Case <code>case.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.vascular-lesion-review.v1</code>; node <code>node.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.flat-vascular-lesion-treatment.v2</code>; question <code>question.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.flat-vascular-lesion-treatment.v2</code>.

- Patient Leonard Price; demographics {"ageYears":74,"sexLabel":"Male"}.
- Complaint: Bleeding treatment review
- Presentation: {patientName}, a 74-year-old man, attends clinic after an outside endoscopic treatment for recurrent lower gastrointestinal bleeding.
- Finite profiles: [{"id":"profile.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.vascular-lesion-review.v1","prototypeDemographics":{"ageYears":74,"sexLabel":"Male"},"chiefComplaint":"Bleeding treatment review","presentation":"{patientName}, a 74-year-old man, attends clinic after an outside endoscopic treatment for recurrent lower gastrointestinal bleeding."}]
- Current update: During prepared colonoscopy, a flat branching red vascular patch in the cecum oozed after washing. A clip stopped a focal point in its center. Further washing showed slow oozing across the remaining flat branching patch beyond the clipped point. The surrounding mucosa was intact and circulation remained stable. Mechanical, injection and thermal devices were available, and the residual patch was accessible.
- Complete task: **Which completed endoscopic plan best fits {patientName}'s post-treatment findings?**

Options ? key shown first for review only:

- **Attempted key** <code>choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.flat-vascular-lesion-treatment.apc.v2</code>: Apply argon plasma coagulation across the residual patch
  Rationale: The remaining flat branching mucosal vascular patch supports angioectasia. APC is an accepted noncontact treatment and is feasible in the recorded examination.
- Distractor <code>choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.flat-vascular-lesion-treatment.clip.v2</code>: Apply further clips across the residual patch
  Rationale: The first clip controlled its point but left distributed superficial oozing. Repeating point control fits the remaining pattern less well than the offered accepted noncontact treatment; clips are not declared ineffective for every vascular lesion.
  Distractor rationale: The first clip controlled its point but left distributed superficial oozing. Repeating point control fits the remaining pattern less well than the offered accepted noncontact treatment; clips are not declared ineffective for every vascular lesion.
- Distractor <code>choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.flat-vascular-lesion-treatment.inject.v2</code>: Inject epinephrine across the residual patch
  Rationale: Injection can provide temporary control but is not the completed definitive plan for this persisting lesion.
  Distractor rationale: Injection can provide temporary control but is not the completed definitive plan for this persisting lesion.

Explanation: The clip controlled one point while an oozing mucosal vascular patch remained. Reassess the residual target instead of equating focal response with complete control. APC is an accepted treatment for bleeding colonic angioectasia; this does not rank every mechanical and thermal method universally.

## Atomic evidence, rights and access

Canonical source records, all 46 atomic claims and bidirectional source/claim/question/field mappings are in <code>docs/research/sources-question-topic-colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding-20261111.json</code>. Two government capability sources and four claims were added, for ten source records. Medical authority and reuse permission remain separate.

ASCRS original successful access remains historical after this round returned 403. Inaccessible AGA pages add no evidence. WSES is CC BY 4.0 with full attribution. Copyrighted ACG guidance was used for targeted verification only; no source prose, tables, figures, algorithms or example cases were copied. PMC availability is not a reuse license. NIDDK procedural text was checked under the government copyright policy, with no graphics, logos or endorsement. A proprietary citation in its reference list was not followed.

Parked attempts and original v1 versions retain audit-only maps. Source links use target=_blank, rel=noopener noreferrer and referrerPolicy=no-referrer. No gameplay network request, model call, hospital setting, capability or order execution was introduced.

## Owner approvals needed

No exact v2 clinical approval or independent PASS is asserted. Parked items remain excluded. Specific clinical questions for Melissa:

- <code>withheld.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.recent-complete-exam-after-abscess</code>; affected . After an abscess with a genuinely recent high-quality complete colonoscopy and no atypical findings, does Melissa want a repeat-examination question keyed to ACG 2026 broader complicated-disease advice or to the more selective ASCRS 2026 framing? Evidence boundary: No scored question asserts a blanket repeat rule for that boundary.
- <code>withheld.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.drainage-borderline-size</code>; affected . Which source-specific pathway should govern a stable abscess near the differing ASCRS 2026 and WSES 2020 size boundaries? Evidence boundary: No borderline cutoff item is keyed. Authored 6-cm collection is beyond both source boundaries.
- <code>withheld.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.diverticular-hemostasis-hierarchy</code>; affected . Confirm current clipping-versus-ligation and direct-versus-indirect clipping rankings against a permitted full ASGE 2026 source before authoring a hierarchy item. Evidence boundary: Current packet compares clipping with temporary injection or no lesion treatment, without competing ligation.
- <code>owner.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.selective-antibiotic-ranking</code>; affected <code>question.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.selected-supportive-care.v1</code>, <code>question.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.immunosuppressed-antibiotic-decision.v1</code>, <code>question.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.selected-supportive-care.v2</code>, <code>question.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.immunosuppressed-antibiotic-decision.v2</code>. In particular review transplant oral-regimen application, selected primary reconstruction, residual endoscopic targets and delayed-scintigraphy localization.

Historical <code>review.n3.postdiverticulitis-examination-extent.v2</code> remains DROP_PROPOSAL. The three additional unkeyed boundaries remain:

- Author difficulty predictions comprise 15 moderate and 10 hard items. These predictions await independent review.

### Remaining research priorities

- **Ischemic colitis and right-sided ischemia escalation** A later bounded research pass should verify a current permitted diagnosis and severity pathway and author a clinic chart-review case. No unsupported key is emitted here.
- **Anticoagulant reversal and resumption after lower-GI bleeding** Verify drug-specific indication, severity and thrombotic-risk boundaries before writing exact regimen or timing questions.
- **Isolated pericolic gas, marginal abscess size and selected purulent-peritonitis lavage** Resolve current source-specific distinctions with Melissa before turning a marginal management boundary into a single-best-answer item.
- **Diverticular wall anatomy, arterial bleeding mechanism, recurrence prevention and persistent pain after recovery** Develop further consequential applied items with permitted atomic sources. Avoid standalone association recall or unsupported recurrence probabilities.

The preparation narrative limits the prior assessment, and his recovered complicated episode supports colonoscopy for an alternative lesion. |
| `choice.n3r2.postdiverticulitis-examination-extent.sigmoidoscopy` |  | Perform flexible sigmoidoscopy with the previous preparation plan | This re-examines the distal region rather than addressing the quality limitation in the earlier colon examination. |

#### Explanation

The prior scope reached the cecum, but preparation prevented adequate inspection of substantial mucosa. Those are different dimensions of examination quality. After this recovered complicated diverticulitis episode, a repeat adequately prepared colonoscopy is the selected luminal evaluation. The prior stop was not a fixed anatomical barrier; no guarantee of completion or universal timing interval is taught.

#### Complaint and presentation

Abdominal pain follow-up

{patientName}, a 49-year-old woman, attends clinic to review her first episode of lower abdominal pain and its outpatient treatment.

One fixed profile `profile.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.first-outpatient-episode.v1` carries this exact age, sex, complaint and presentation.

#### Current update

At that visit she had left-lower-quadrant tenderness, a low-grade fever and discomfort during urination. Urinalysis showed a few leukocytes without nitrites or blood. Her abdomen was soft outside the tender area. She had never had similar pain or abdominal imaging. Creatinine was within the laboratory reference interval.

#### Exhibit

?

#### Complete task

Which investigation best fits {patientName}'s initial presentation?

#### Options and feedback

Key shown first for review only.

| Choice | Key | Label | Rationale |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.first-presentation-ct.contrast-ct.v1` | key | Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis | The first episode has overlapping urinary and colonic features. Abdominopelvic CT can establish the source and assess for a collection or other complication. |
| `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.first-presentation-ct.stone-ct.v1` |  | Noncontrast CT using a ureteric-stone protocol | The urinary discomfort can accompany adjacent colonic inflammation. The focal abdominal findings and uncertain first episode call for assessment of bowel inflammation and complications, beyond a stone-focused examination. |
| `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.first-presentation-ct.colonoscopy.v1` |  | Colonoscopy with inspection of the entire colon | Colonoscopy may have a later role in luminal assessment. It does not supply the initial cross-sectional assessment of a possible acute extraluminal inflammatory complication. |

The urinary findings do not establish the source of pain. For a first suspected colonic inflammatory episode, CT can confirm the diagnosis and evaluate its extent.

#### Clinical reasoning and deletion check

- Interpret. Interpret mild urinary findings alongside focal abdominal inflammation without declaring the urinary tract to be the source.
- Apply. Choose a cross-sectional study that evaluates bowel and adjacent structures during a first uncertain episode.
- Closest competing choice `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.first-presentation-ct.stone-ct.v1`. The focal left-lower abdominal syndrome has no hematuria or characteristic renal-colic course.
- Consequence. A stone-focused pathway can leave an inflammatory complication insufficiently characterized.
- Counterfactual. Replace focal left-lower tenderness and fever with abrupt colicky flank pain radiating to the groin and hematuria. A stone-protocol CT becomes reasonable among these choices. The resulting competing choice is `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.first-presentation-ct.stone-ct.v1`.
- Deletion check. Urinary discomfort earns the stone competitor. First-episode status earns confirmation. Renal function supplies contrast context. Further routine history was removed.
- Sequence check. First node. Feedback identifies the value of CT and supplies no antibiotic-eligibility rule for the next node.

#### Five author checks

1. **Cover-the-key cue attack** The complaint and task name no diagnosis or protocol. All options are specific studies. Both CT choices have the same placeholder profile, and colonoscopy has its own estimate.
2. **One decision stage and category** Three initial investigations for the same unresolved source of pain.
3. **Two consequential reasoning steps** Interpret mild urinary findings alongside focal abdominal inflammation without declaring the urinary tract to be the source. Choose a cross-sectional study that evaluates bowel and adjacent structures during a first uncertain episode.
4. **Predicted resident difficulty** moderate. The resident must resist urinary anchoring and select the acquisition appropriate to the broader clinical problem.
5. **One defensible key and counterfactual** The focal left-lower abdominal syndrome has no hematuria or characteristic renal-colic course. Replace focal left-lower tenderness and fever with abrupt colicky flank pain radiating to the groin and hematuria. A stone-protocol CT becomes reasonable among these choices. Review boundary. Protocol detail is a qualitative clinical application of the CT guidance. Exact wording and acquisition ranking require clinician review.

#### Complaint and presentation

Abdominal pain follow-up

{patientName}, a 49-year-old woman, attends clinic to review her first episode of lower abdominal pain and its outpatient treatment.

One fixed profile `profile.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.first-outpatient-episode.v1` carries this exact age, sex, complaint and presentation.

#### Current update

CT showed sigmoid wall thickening and adjacent fat stranding, with no collection, extraluminal gas or obstruction. By reassessment her pain was improving, pulse was 78/min and temperature 37.1 C. She drank and ate without vomiting, took no immunosuppressive medicine and managed her usual activities independently. She could return for reassessment. Her history included two antibiotic-associated C. difficile infections.

#### Exhibit

?

#### Complete task

Which initial outpatient plan best fits {patientName}'s CT findings and subsequent assessment?

#### Options and feedback

Key shown first for review only.

| Choice | Key | Label | Rationale |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.selected-supportive-care.support.v1` | key | Use oral hydration and analgesia with early reassessment | The CT and observed course support a selected nonantibiotic outpatient plan. Give explicit return instructions for worsening pain, fever or inability to maintain intake. |
| `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.selected-supportive-care.amoxicillin.v1` |  | Start oral amoxicillin-clavulanate with early reassessment | Antibiotics remain appropriate for higher-risk or worsening disease. Here the mild improving course meets selective omission criteria, and prior C. difficile increases the cost of avoidable antibiotic exposure. |
| `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.selected-supportive-care.admit.v1` |  | Use inpatient intravenous antibiotics with serial reassessment | Admission is appropriate when illness severity or oral-intake failure warrants it. Her current trajectory and oral tolerance support outpatient care. |

Her CT and clinical trajectory support selective omission of antibiotics. Previous C. difficile makes unnecessary exposure consequential. Outpatient care still includes reassessment and return instructions.

#### Clinical reasoning and deletion check

- Interpret. Combine the absence of a CT complication with the actual improving course and ability to maintain intake.
- Apply. Choose selective nonantibiotic care while weighing the patient's prior antibiotic-associated harm.
- Closest competing choice `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.selected-supportive-care.amoxicillin.v1`. Mild improving uncomplicated disease in an independent immunocompetent outpatient with previous C. difficile.
- Consequence. Routine treatment adds avoidable antibiotic exposure to a patient with a relevant prior complication.
- Counterfactual. Replace immune competence with active transplant immunosuppression while retaining oral tolerance and stability. Oral antibiotic treatment becomes the better plan among the offered choices. The resulting competing choice is `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.selected-supportive-care.amoxicillin.v1`.
- Deletion check. CT determines complication status. Oral intake and reassessment establish disposition. Independence and medicine history establish eligibility. Prior C. difficile distinguishes an otherwise defensible antibiotic option.
- Sequence check. The CT explanation does not teach the omission criteria. The current clinical course, immune history and prior harm enter only at this node.

#### Five author checks

1. **Cover-the-key cue attack** Removed the summary labels nonfrail and eligible for no antibiotics. Options have comparable follow-up scope. Prior infection is a legitimate patient-specific harm, recorded for independent review.
2. **One decision stage and category** Three initial care plans with the same reassessment obligation.
3. **Two consequential reasoning steps** Combine the absence of a CT complication with the actual improving course and ability to maintain intake. Choose selective nonantibiotic care while weighing the patient's prior antibiotic-associated harm.
4. **Predicted resident difficulty** moderate. The resident must apply omission criteria and resist routine antibiotics despite a confirmed inflammatory diagnosis.
5. **One defensible key and counterfactual** Mild improving uncomplicated disease in an independent immunocompetent outpatient with previous C. difficile. Replace immune competence with active transplant immunosuppression while retaining oral tolerance and stability. Oral antibiotic treatment becomes the better plan among the offered choices. Review boundary. Guidance permits selective omission rather than forbidding antibiotics. Clinician review must confirm the patient-specific ranking against oral amoxicillin-clavulanate.

#### Complaint and presentation

Recovery planning

{patientName}, a 58-year-old man, attends clinic after treatment of his first sigmoid diverticular abscess at an outside hospital.

One fixed profile `profile.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.recovered-abscess.v1` carries this exact age, sex, complaint and presentation.

#### Current update

Drainage and antibiotics resolved his fever and focal tenderness. Follow-up CT documented collapse of the collection and resolution of adjacent inflammation. He had returned to his usual bowel pattern. His only prior endoscopy report described the esophagus, stomach and duodenum. His records contained no colorectal screening examination.

#### Exhibit

?

#### Complete task

Which investigation should {patientName}'s post-recovery plan include?

#### Options and feedback

Key shown first for review only.

| Choice | Key | Label | Rationale |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.post-abscess-colonoscopy.colonoscopy.v1` | key | Arrange complete colonoscopy at follow-up | The prior upper examination did not assess the colon. This recovered abscess episode and absent colorectal examination support colonoscopy for an alternative lesion. |
| `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.post-abscess-colonoscopy.ct.v1` |  | Repeat contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis | CT has already documented collection resolution. Another routine scan would not supply the outstanding mucosal evaluation after this recovered abscess. |
| `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.post-abscess-colonoscopy.stool.v1` |  | Obtain a fecal immunochemical test at follow-up | A stool blood test does not replace the indicated direct examination of the colon in this post-abscess assessment. |

Clinical and CT recovery address the abscess. The earlier endoscopy assessed the upper tract. A complete colonic examination remains indicated in this patient after the complicated episode.

#### Clinical reasoning and deletion check

- Interpret. Separate collection resolution from assessment of the colonic lumen, and identify the actual extent of the earlier endoscopy.
- Apply. Select colonoscopy for the outstanding post-recovery evaluation.
- Closest competing choice `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.post-abscess-colonoscopy.ct.v1`. The collection has resolved, but no prior examination evaluated the colon.
- Consequence. Repeating the extraluminal study can leave a relevant mucosal lesion unassessed.
- Counterfactual. Replace recovery and a collapsed collection with recurrent fever and focal tenderness after drainage. Repeat CT becomes the initial reassessment among these options. The resulting competing choice is `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.post-abscess-colonoscopy.ct.v1`.
- Deletion check. Clinical recovery makes this an interval evaluation. CT completion removes redundant imaging. The documented upper examination establishes organ provenance. No fixed interval was retained.
- Sequence check. First node. Feedback addresses colonic evaluation and gives no elective surgery rule.

#### Five author checks

1. **Cover-the-key cue attack** The complaint and task do not name colonoscopy. All three options are investigations with estimates. The wrong-site history adds an inference without an unsupported repeat-modality hierarchy.
2. **One decision stage and category** Three investigations proposed at the same recovered follow-up visit.
3. **Two consequential reasoning steps** Separate collection resolution from assessment of the colonic lumen, and identify the actual extent of the earlier endoscopy. Select colonoscopy for the outstanding post-recovery evaluation.
4. **Predicted resident difficulty** moderate. Two apparently reassuring completed investigations must be interpreted for the question each actually answered.
5. **One defensible key and counterfactual** The collection has resolved, but no prior examination evaluated the colon. Replace recovery and a collapsed collection with recurrent fever and focal tenderness after drainage. Repeat CT becomes the initial reassessment among these options. Review boundary. The stool-test foil is weaker for an experienced resident. This replacement retains a core existing objective and needs independent difficulty review.

| `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.post-abscess-colonoscopy.ct.v1` | Treating radiologic resolution of the inflammatory complication as the only required follow-up endpoint. | Persistent symptoms or infection raise concern for an unresolved collection or another extraluminal complication. | `claim.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.recovery-colonoscopy`<br>`claim.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.failure-source-control` |
| `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.post-abscess-colonoscopy.colonoscopy.v1` | Distinguishing an endoscopy heading from the actual organ examined. | A recovered complicated episode leaves an indicated colonic examination outstanding. | `claim.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.recovery-colonoscopy` |
| `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.post-abscess-colonoscopy.stool.v1` | Substituting a screening tool for diagnostic follow-up of a complicated colonic episode. | An otherwise suitable average-risk screening patient is choosing a stool-based screening pathway. | `claim.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.recovery-colonoscopy` |

#### Complaint and presentation

Recovery planning

{patientName}, a 58-year-old man, attends clinic after treatment of his first sigmoid diverticular abscess at an outside hospital.

One fixed profile `profile.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.recovered-abscess.v1` carries this exact age, sex, complaint and presentation.

#### Current update

Colonoscopy found no mucosal mass. During later follow-up he had another CT-confirmed inflammatory episode, with symptom-free recovery between episodes. The episodes repeatedly interrupted work. His current CT showed resolution, he exercised without limitation, and preoperative assessment identified no major cardiopulmonary disease. After discussing operative complications and possible persistent symptoms, he preferred resection to further recurrences.

#### Exhibit

?

#### Complete task

Which treatment plan best fits {patientName}'s subsequent clinic assessment?

#### Options and feedback

It is not triggered by a required episode count. |
| `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.elective-burden-after-abscess.observe.v1` |  | Continue nonoperative follow-up for future episodes | Observation remains a valid option after recovery. His recurrent burden, operative assessment and informed preference now support offering a specific elective operation. |
| `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.elective-burden-after-abscess.mesalamine.v1` |  | Start oral mesalamine maintenance therapy | Maintenance mesalamine is not a supported substitute for the elective decision in recurrent diverticular disease. |

Elective resection can be offered after recovery when burden, operative risk and an informed patient's priorities support it. It reduces recurrence risk while carrying operative and persistent-symptom risks. Episode count does not supply the decision.

#### Clinical reasoning and deletion check

- Interpret. Identify discrete recovered recurrences with substantial functional burden rather than ongoing uncontrolled infection.
- Apply. Choose a concrete elective resection plan consistent with acceptable risk and informed preference.
- Closest competing choice `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.elective-burden-after-abscess.observe.v1`. Repeated work interruption and a preference for surgery after an explicit risk discussion, with recovery and acceptable operative assessment.
- Consequence. A fixed policy of waiting leaves the patient's recurrent burden untreated despite an appropriate elective option.
- Counterfactual. Replace work interruption and the operative preference with no current symptoms, substantial operative risk and a preference to avoid surgery. Nonoperative follow-up becomes the better option. The resulting competing choice is `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.elective-burden-after-abscess.observe.v1`.
- Deletion check. Interval recovery distinguishes elective treatment from source control. Function and risk establish the tradeoff. Informed preference is necessary because two reasonable strategies otherwise remain.
- Sequence check. The prior explanation addresses colonic evaluation. New recurrence burden, operative assessment and informed preference determine this node.

#### Five author checks

1. **Cover-the-key cue attack** Removed generic shared-decision labels and episode-count caricatures. The preference earns its place as the legitimate tie-breaker. All labels name actual treatment plans.
2. **One decision stage and category** Three elective strategies after resolution of acute infection.
3. **Two consequential reasoning steps** Identify discrete recovered recurrences with substantial functional burden rather than ongoing uncontrolled infection. Choose a concrete elective resection plan consistent with acceptable risk and informed preference.
4. **Predicted resident difficulty** moderate. The resident must apply conditional guidance to a concrete decision instead of repeating that counseling is individualized.
5. **One defensible key and counterfactual** Repeated work interruption and a preference for surgery after an explicit risk discussion, with recovery and acceptable operative assessment. Replace work interruption and the operative preference with no current symptoms, substantial operative risk and a preference to avoid surgery. Nonoperative follow-up becomes the better option. Review boundary. This changes the old discussion objective to treatment selection and therefore uses a new concept version. It cannot inherit the old FSRS identity or approval.

#### Complaint and presentation

Urinary infection review

{patientName}, a 64-year-old man, attends clinic to review outside records of recurrent urinary symptoms and lower abdominal pain.

One fixed profile `profile.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.urinary-symptoms.v1` carries this exact age, sex, complaint and presentation.

#### Current update

Cultured urinary infections recurred after appropriate treatment. He described bubbles during urination and left-lower-quadrant discomfort. Examination found focal abdominal tenderness. There had been no urinary catheterization or abdominal imaging, and he had no prior imaging-confirmed colonic diagnosis.

#### Exhibit

?

#### Complete task

Which investigation best addresses {patientName}'s initial combination of findings?

#### Options and feedback

Key shown first for review only.

| Choice | Key | Label | Rationale |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.first-episode-with-urinary-symptoms.ct.v1` | key | Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis | The urinary and abdominal findings raise concern for a connected pelvic process. CT evaluates bowel inflammation, adjacent bladder involvement and other complications. |
| `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.first-episode-with-urinary-symptoms.cystoscopy.v1` |  | Cystoscopy to inspect the bladder lumen | Cystoscopy can assess a bladder lesion, but it does not supply the initial cross-sectional assessment of an adjacent colonic inflammatory source. |
| `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.first-episode-with-urinary-symptoms.ultrasound.v1` |  | Ultrasound of the kidneys and bladder | Ultrasound can assess urinary obstruction but may leave the neighboring bowel process and its extent unresolved. |

Recurrent urinary infection with bubbles during urination and focal lower abdominal tenderness requires assessment of adjacent bowel and bladder. CT supplies that cross-sectional evaluation.

#### Clinical reasoning and deletion check

- Interpret. Recognize that repeated urinary infection with gas symptoms may arise from an adjacent bowel process.
- Apply. Choose an initial study that evaluates the source and its extraluminal extent.
- Closest competing choice `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.first-episode-with-urinary-symptoms.cystoscopy.v1`. Gas symptoms and focal abdominal tenderness accompany recurrent culture-proven infection without instrumentation.
- Consequence. Bladder-focused inspection may postpone characterization of the diseased bowel and pelvic connection.
- Counterfactual. Replace the gas symptoms and abdominal tenderness with persistent painless hematuria after adequate normal cross-sectional imaging. Bladder inspection becomes the appropriate offered next study. The resulting competing choice is `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.first-episode-with-urinary-symptoms.cystoscopy.v1`.
- Deletion check. Recurrent cultures distinguish one uncomplicated urinary infection. Gas symptoms and no instrumentation support the communication concern. The abdominal localization makes a bowel assessment consequential.
- Sequence check. The first explanation identifies the assessment need. It does not name a later operation or guarantee a diagnosis.

#### Five author checks

1. **Cover-the-key cue attack** The full context avoids the names fistula and diverticulitis before answering. All options are credible urinary/pelvic investigations with individual timing records.
2. **One decision stage and category** Three initial investigations of the same unresolved pelvic source.
3. **Two consequential reasoning steps** Recognize that repeated urinary infection with gas symptoms may arise from an adjacent bowel process. Choose an initial study that evaluates the source and its extraluminal extent.
4. **Predicted resident difficulty** moderate. The resident must integrate findings across organ systems and choose the initial acquisition rather than merely label the communication.
5. **One defensible key and counterfactual** Gas symptoms and focal abdominal tenderness accompany recurrent culture-proven infection without instrumentation. Replace the gas symptoms and abdominal tenderness with persistent painless hematuria after adequate normal cross-sectional imaging. Bladder inspection becomes the appropriate offered next study. Review boundary. The fistula pattern is familiar. Difficulty comes from CT versus cystoscopy sequencing and needs independent clinical review.

Admission decision review

{patientName}, a 55-year-old woman, attends clinic after an outside admission for lower abdominal pain and fever.

CT showed sigmoid inflammation and a rim-enhancing pelvic collection measuring 6 cm. There was no diffuse free fluid or remote gas. She had focal tenderness without generalized guarding, and blood pressure remained stable after fluid replacement. The interventional radiology review documented a percutaneous route that avoided bowel. Intravenous antibiotics had been started.

?

The resulting competing choice is `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.large-accessible-abscess.antibiotics.v1`.
- Deletion check. Size distinguishes the antibiotic-only competitor. The route review establishes actual access rather than permission wording. Physiology and examination distinguish drainage from immediate resection.
- Sequence check. Feedback explains the initial source-control choice without supplying a future operative failure rule.

#### Complaint and presentation

Admission decision review

{patientName}, a 55-year-old woman, attends clinic after an outside admission for lower abdominal pain and fever.

One fixed profile `profile.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.pelvic-abscess-course.v1` carries this exact age, sex, complaint and presentation.

#### Current update

After drainage, she developed increasing fever, tachycardia and broader abdominal tenderness despite antibiotics active against the cultured organisms. Repeat CT showed the drained cavity had collapsed, but another rim-enhancing collection had enlarged between bowel loops. The existing drain entered the collapsed cavity. Interventional review found no percutaneous path to the enlarging collection that avoided bowel.

#### Exhibit

?

#### Complete task

Which next hospital plan best fits {patientName}'s changed course?

#### Options and feedback

Key shown first for review only.

| Choice | Key | Label | Rationale |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.failed-abscess-source-control.operate.v1` | key | Proceed to operative control of the undrained source | The patient is worsening with an enlarging collection despite active antibiotics. The current drain misses that space and a safe percutaneous rescue route is absent. |
| `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.failed-abscess-source-control.broaden.v1` |  | Broaden antibiotics and continue the current drain plan | The organisms are already covered. The changed anatomy and clinical deterioration point to inadequate source control rather than a documented antimicrobial mismatch. |
| `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.failed-abscess-source-control.upsize.v1` |  | Exchange the existing drain for a larger catheter | The catheter reaches a collapsed cavity. Increasing its size does not establish access to the separate enlarging collection. |

The new collection lies outside the drained space. The combination of clinical worsening and an inaccessible enlarging source supports operative source control. A larger catheter in the collapsed cavity does not repair the anatomic mismatch.

#### Clinical reasoning and deletion check

- Interpret. Distinguish collapse of one drained cavity from control of a separate infected space.
- Apply. Escalate to operative source control after a technically defined nonoperative failure.
- Closest competing choice `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.failed-abscess-source-control.upsize.v1`. The catheter and enlarging collection occupy different spaces, with no safe percutaneous access to the latter.
- Consequence. Repeated manipulation of the wrong cavity can delay source control during clinical deterioration.
- Counterfactual. Replace the separate inaccessible collection with residual fluid communicating with an obstructed catheter. Drain exchange or upsizing becomes a reasonable rescue step. The resulting competing choice is `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.failed-abscess-source-control.upsize.v1`.
- Deletion check. Culture activity tests the antibiotic-breadth error. The cavity map and catheter tip are essential. The worsening clinical course gives the unresolved anatomy a management consequence.
- Sequence check. The initial drainage decision supplies neither the new separate cavity nor the route limitation. Deleting this update removes the operative indication.

#### Five author checks

1. **Cover-the-key cue attack** The task does not name source-control failure. All options are specific treatment changes. No elapsed-time deadline or generic failure label supplies the answer.
2. **One decision stage and category** Three rescue treatment plans after a documented drainage attempt.
3. **Two consequential reasoning steps** Distinguish collapse of one drained cavity from control of a separate infected space. Escalate to operative source control after a technically defined nonoperative failure.
4. **Predicted resident difficulty** hard. The resident must integrate microbiology, drain position, separate-space anatomy and actual deterioration.
5. **One defensible key and counterfactual** The catheter and enlarging collection occupy different spaces, with no safe percutaneous access to the latter. Replace the separate inaccessible collection with residual fluid communicating with an obstructed catheter. Drain exchange or upsizing becomes a reasonable rescue step. Review boundary. Exact operative technique is deliberately left to the treating surgeon. Guidelines support escalation but provide no universal clock or catheter-size rule.

| `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.failed-abscess-source-control.upsize.v1` | Equating catheter caliber with drainage of every adjacent space. | The remaining infected collection communicates with the catheter and catheter obstruction or size limits drainage. | `claim.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.failure-source-control`<br>`claim.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.abscess-drainage` |

#### Complaint and presentation

Operation review

{patientName}, a 46-year-old man, attends clinic after emergency abdominal surgery at an outside hospital. The founder reviews the sequential operative records with him.

One fixed profile `profile.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.perforation-operative-review.v1` carries this exact age, sex, complaint and presentation.

#### Current update

After resuscitation, exploration found a disrupted sigmoid diverticulum with a visible full-thickness opening and liquid stool in several abdominal compartments. The remaining colon was viable. Broad-spectrum antibiotics had already been given.

#### Exhibit

?

#### Complete task

Which source-control procedure best fits {patientName}'s initial operative findings?

#### Options and feedback

Key shown first for review only.

| Choice | Key | Label | Rationale |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.gross-perforation-source-control.resection.v1` | key | Resect the perforated diseased sigmoid segment | The gross perforation and fecal contamination favor removal of the diseased source. |
| `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.gross-perforation-source-control.lavage.v1` |  | Perform peritoneal lavage and place abdominal drains | A visible perforation with diffuse fecal contamination requires control of the diseased bowel source. Evidence for selected lavage in purulent disease does not support this feculent presentation. |
| `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.gross-perforation-source-control.repair.v1` |  | Close the visible opening and place abdominal drains | Simple closure leaves the diseased sigmoid segment in a setting requiring definitive source control. A limited repair strategy has a different role in selected damage-control circumstances. |

The operative findings establish a gross perforation with fecal contamination. Colectomy addresses the diseased source. Reconstruction is considered separately after resection and assessment of physiology and bowel condition.

#### Clinical reasoning and deletion check

- Interpret. Distinguish a gross fecal leak from contained gas or selected purulent peritonitis.
- Apply. Choose definitive colonic source control at the current operation.
- Closest competing choice `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.gross-perforation-source-control.lavage.v1`. A visible full-thickness sigmoid opening accompanies liquid stool across abdominal compartments.
- Consequence. A lavage-based plan can leave the continuing fecal source uncontrolled.
- Counterfactual. Replace gross perforation and fecal contamination with a selected purulent-peritonitis presentation without a visible opening. Lavage becomes a possible specialist option requiring explicit clinical review. The resulting competing choice is `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.gross-perforation-source-control.lavage.v1`.
- Deletion check. The visible opening and contamination type earn the distinction. Viability defines the source-control scope. Antibiotics are shared care and keep the choice at the procedural stage.
- Sequence check. Feedback separates source control from reconstruction and gives no answer-specific anastomotic eligibility criteria.

#### Five author checks

1. **Cover-the-key cue attack** All options are operative source-control procedures with parallel verbs. The complaint and task do not name a diagnosis grade or a preferred method. Contamination remains essential raw evidence.
2. **One decision stage and category** Three source-control procedures before a reconstruction decision.
3. **Two consequential reasoning steps** Distinguish a gross fecal leak from contained gas or selected purulent peritonitis. Choose definitive colonic source control at the current operation.
4. **Predicted resident difficulty** moderate. The challenge is applying the limits of a less invasive strategy to the actual operative findings.
5. **One defensible key and counterfactual** A visible full-thickness sigmoid opening accompanies liquid stool across abdominal compartments. Replace gross perforation and fecal contamination with a selected purulent-peritonitis presentation without a visible opening. Lavage becomes a possible specialist option requiring explicit clinical review. Review boundary. The counterfactual makes lavage potentially reasonable and does not claim it becomes universally preferred. This high-acuity decision is displayed as retrospective clinic chart review.

| `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.gross-perforation-source-control.lavage.v1` | Generalizing a selected nonresection strategy to any generalized diverticular contamination. | A carefully selected purulent-peritonitis case without gross perforation is being considered by an experienced team under the appropriate evidence boundary. | `claim.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.gross-perforation-resection` |
| `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.gross-perforation-source-control.repair.v1` | Treating the visible hole as an isolated defect independent of the diseased segment. | A selected limited injury or staged damage-control situation supports a deliberately abbreviated repair. | `claim.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.gross-perforation-resection`<br>`claim.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.hartmann-high-risk` |

- Counterfactual. Replace stable physiology and healthy host conditions with persistent vasopressor dependence, major comorbidity and edematous bowel. - Deletion check. Each host and bowel observation addresses an actual anastomotic eligibility dimension. The specific surgeon role records provenance. No generic phrase saying suitable for anastomosis was used.
- Sequence check. Source-control feedback cannot choose the reconstruction without the new physiology and bowel findings. These data are withheld until this stage.

5. **One defensible key and counterfactual** Stable unsupported circulation, acceptable host condition and perfused tension-free bowel ends. Replace stable physiology and healthy host conditions with persistent vasopressor dependence, major comorbidity and edematous bowel. Hartmann reconstruction becomes the preferred offered definitive reconstruction if the team proceeds with definitive surgery. Review boundary. Guidelines support consideration under selected conditions. Hartmann may remain defensible for reasons absent from a short record, so Melissa must confirm the intended ranking.

#### Complaint and presentation

Treatment follow-up

{patientName}, a 68-year-old woman, attends clinic after outpatient treatment of her first CT-confirmed sigmoid inflammatory episode. She receives tacrolimus and mycophenolate after a kidney transplant.

One fixed profile `profile.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.immunosuppressed-recovery.v1` carries this exact age, sex, complaint and presentation.

#### Current update

At that visit CT showed focal sigmoid wall thickening and fat inflammation without a collection or free perforation. Pulse and blood pressure were normal, she ate without vomiting and pain was controlled with oral medication. Tacrolimus and mycophenolate had been continued throughout the illness. She had no penicillin allergy, renal function was preserved, and an early reassessment visit was arranged.

#### Exhibit

?

#### Complete task

Which initial care plan best fits {patientName}'s acute assessment?

#### Options and feedback

Key shown first for review only.

| `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.immunosuppressed-antibiotic-decision.oral-antibiotic.v1` | key | Start oral amoxicillin-clavulanate with outpatient reassessment | Her immune status supports antibiotics despite limited CT disease. The supplied stability, oral tolerance and reassessment plan support an oral outpatient approach. |
| `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.immunosuppressed-antibiotic-decision.support.v1` |  | Use oral hydration and analgesia with outpatient reassessment | The reassuring CT and oral tolerance do not place a chronically immunosuppressed patient within the usual nonantibiotic-trial population. |
| `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.immunosuppressed-antibiotic-decision.inpatient.v1` |  | Arrange inpatient intravenous antibiotic treatment and observation | Hospital treatment is appropriate for deterioration, systemic illness, oral-intake failure or unsafe follow-up. Those features are not supplied by this stable assessment. |

Immune suppression changes antibiotic eligibility even when CT shows limited disease. Route and disposition still follow the actual clinical assessment. In this constructed stable orally tolerant patient, the proposed plan is oral antibiotic treatment with early reassessment.

#### Clinical reasoning and deletion check

- Interpret. Distinguish uncomplicated imaging from membership in the immunocompetent antibiotic-omission population.
- Apply. Select antibiotic treatment and then match its route to the observed stability and intake.
- Closest competing choice `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.immunosuppressed-antibiotic-decision.support.v1`. Antirejection therapy after kidney transplantation continues during an otherwise stable orally tolerant episode.
- Consequence. Applying omission data to an excluded host can undertreat a patient at higher complication concern.
- Counterfactual. Remove immunosuppression and retain mild disease, oral tolerance, stability and reliable review. Supportive outpatient care becomes reasonable among the offered plans. The resulting competing choice is `choice.topic.colon-diverticular-lower-bleeding.immunosuppressed-antibiotic-decision.support.v1`.
- Deletion check. Immune status determines treatment eligibility. Vitals, intake and follow-up determine route and disposition. Allergy and renal context support the named medicine without adding an invented dose.
- Sequence check. First node. Feedback discusses acute antibiotic eligibility and gives no prophylactic elective-operation policy.

2. **One decision stage and category** Three initial treatment/disposition plans for the acute episode.

Remove immunosuppression and retain mild disease, oral tolerance, stability and reliable review. Supportive outpatient care becomes reasonable among the offered plans. Review boundary. Oral outpatient treatment in a chronically immunosuppressed patient is patient-specific. One checked highlight supports the named oral regimen. Exact severity and disposition ranking need Melissa's review.
